# Would the white car hit anyone in the group if it drove forward?

**Short answer: No. If the white SUV pulled straight forward it would drive off to the right across the sand, passing well behind the group of people. It would not hit any of them.**

Below is the reasoning, stated point by point.

## 1. What is in the picture

The photo is taken from a sandy rise (a dune of pale sand fills the whole lower half of the frame) looking out over a hazy sea, with a distant low coastal town visible on the far left. Just below the skyline there is a white full-size SUV (it looks like a Chevrolet Tahoe / GMC Yukon type vehicle) parked on the sand, with one of its side doors standing open — the dark opening with a seat visible inside is clear at high magnification.

To the right of the vehicle in the frame stands a loose cluster of about seven adults, all facing out towards the sea/view rather than towards the camera: a woman in a white top, sunglasses and a green skirt; a man in a black printed T-shirt and black cap with olive cargo trousers; a partly hidden person in a pale blue shirt and khaki shorts; a man in a grey shirt and cap with light trousers; a person in a teal top; an older man with white hair in a yellow polo shirt with a hand raised to his face; and a man in a dark striped polo shirt. Everybody's feet are cut off at a sharp horizontal sand line, because a nearer ridge of sand hides their lower legs.

## 2. Which way the car is facing

The car's **rear is at the left of the frame and it is facing to the right.** This is unambiguous at high zoom:

- There is a tall, narrow **vertical red tail-light cluster** at the left-hand end of the body — the signature vertical rear lamp of that generation of Tahoe/Yukon. Headlights on that vehicle are wide and horizontal, and are not red.
- Below it there is a **rear step bumper** protruding at the left-hand corner.
- The left-hand end also shows the **dark tinted liftgate/rear quarter glass** and the rear-quarter badge, and the roofline curves down into the tailgate there.
- The rear wheel sits close to that left-hand end with a short overhang; the second (front) wheel is further right, roughly 80 px away, which matches the vehicle's wheelbase.

So "forward" for this car means **towards the right-hand side of the photograph**, i.e. in the same 2-D direction as the group.

## 3. But the car is almost side-on to the camera, and the group is much closer to the camera

Two separate measurements matter here.

**(a) The car is essentially broadside.** Its apparent length (rear bumper to front end, ~130 px) versus its apparent height (~45 px for a vehicle about 1.9 m tall) gives a length-to-height ratio of about 2.9, against a true ratio of about 2.7 for such an SUV. Front and rear tyres are the same apparent width (about 22 px each) and their ground contacts are at the same height in the frame. All of this says the vehicle's long axis is very nearly perpendicular to the camera's line of sight — it is parked side-on, pointing right, within perhaps ten degrees either way. Therefore "driving forward" carries it **sideways across the picture, staying at roughly its own distance from the camera**, not towards the viewer.

**(b) The people are roughly twice as close to the camera as the car is.** This is the decisive point, and it is easy to check:

- The SUV, which is about 1.9 m tall, measures only about 45 px from roof to ground in the image — a scale of roughly 23–25 pixels per metre. Its wheelbase, beltline height and tyre diameter all agree with that figure.
- The adults in the group measure about 80–100 px from head to the sand line — a scale of roughly 45–55 pixels per metre, i.e. about twice as large.
- Equivalently: the people's heads stand about 47 px **above the roofline of the SUV**, while their legs run down to the same sand line as its wheels. A person standing beside that vehicle would have their head *below* its roof, since the SUV is taller than a person. For their heads to clear the roof by that much while at the car's distance, they would have to be three to four metres tall.

The only consistent reading is that the group is standing well in front of the car, between it and the photographer — on the order of ten metres closer, with the car perhaps 20–25 m from the camera and the group around 10 m. Their feet are hidden because the sand ridge in the foreground cuts them off, which is why they *appear* to stand on the same ground line as the wheels.

## 4. Putting it together

In plan view, the car sits on a line running left–right across the scene, nose pointing right. The group is clustered off to the right **and a long way nearer the camera**. Driving straight ahead, the car would track to the right at its own depth and pass roughly ten metres behind the whole group — behind even the furthest-away member of it, the man in the dark striped polo on the far right, who is still only about half as far away as the vehicle.

The overlaps in the photo are line-of-sight overlaps only. The woman in the green skirt looks as though she is standing in the open doorway, and the man in the black T-shirt looks as though he is leaning on the front wing, but both are simply in front of those parts of the car from the camera's viewpoint; they are metres away from the bodywork in reality.

Even allowing generously for error — say the car's nose is angled as much as 20–25° towards the camera rather than truly broadside, and the group is only 1.5× nearer rather than 2× — the car would have to travel something like 15–20 m forward before reaching the group's depth, by which time it would be far to the right of everyone in the frame. There is no plausible geometry consistent with this image in which pulling forward puts the vehicle into the people.

## 5. Caveats

- The car's actual front bumper and nose are hidden behind the nearer people, so its exact heading has a few degrees of uncertainty; the conclusion is robust to that, as shown above.
- This answers the question for the seven visible people. Anyone out of frame, or anyone who walked into the vehicle's path after the shutter fired, is obviously not covered.
